items.prompt: In the dinner party picture, tasting one ingredient matches which test level?
choices: Unit test
Integration test
End-to-end test
Smoke screening
items.explanation: A spoonful checks one part on its own, which is what a unit test does with one function.

items.prompt: Which level lets real components talk to each other and checks the result?
choices: Unit test
Integration test
End-to-end test
Style review
items.explanation: Integration tests run real components together, like cooking one dish with all its ingredients.

items.prompt: Which level drives a whole user-facing flow the way a person would?
choices: Unit test
Integration test
Spot check
End-to-end test
items.explanation: An end-to-end test is the full rehearsal: it walks the entire flow from start to finish.

items.prompt: A test calls one pure function with fixed inputs and touches no network. Which level is it?
choices: Integration test
Unit test
End-to-end test
Acceptance rehearsal
items.explanation: One function, no collaborators: that is a unit test.

items.prompt: Which of the three levels is normally the slowest to run?
choices: Unit tests
Integration tests
End-to-end tests
They all take equal time
items.explanation: The more of the system a test starts and drives, the longer it takes, so end-to-end tests are the slowest.

items.prompt: When a unit test fails, what does the failure usually tell you?
choices: Which function or module is wrong
That some part of the app is broken
That the network is unreliable
That the browser needs updating
items.explanation: A unit test covers one small thing, so a failure names that thing.

items.prompt: Which description fits an end-to-end test?
choices: It checks one function in isolation
It checks two real components against each other
It replaces every dependency with a stand-in
It runs a complete flow as a user would
items.explanation: End-to-end means from the user's first action to the final visible result.

items.prompt: Are unit, integration and end-to-end tests a ranking from worst to best?
choices: No, each one answers a different question
Yes, end-to-end is always the best of the three
Yes, unit tests are always the best of the three
No, only integration tests are real tests
items.explanation: They are different tools. The skill is matching the question to the level.

items.prompt: A test starts a real local database, saves an order, then reads it back to check the row. Which level is it?
choices: A unit test, since only the save function is exercised
An integration test, since two real parts must cooperate
An end-to-end test, since the data ends up stored for later
A unit test, since databases are only fancy variables
items.explanation: The save code and the database are two real parts working together, which is the integration level. It is not end-to-end because no user flow is driven.
items.reference:
Three sizes of check
unit: taste one ingredient (one function, alone)
integration: cook one dish (real parts together)
end-to-end: rehearse the party (the whole flow)
Why: each level answers a different question, so none of them is simply better.
items.learnMore:
Unit, integration and end-to-end

A unit test isolates one function or module. An integration test lets real components talk to each other. An end-to-end test drives the whole system the way a user would. Each sees something the others cannot.

Common mistake

Treating the levels as a ranking from weak to strong instead of three different questions.
items.reflection: Think of a project outside software with a small check, a medium check and a full dress rehearsal. What does each one catch that the others would miss?

items.prompt: A test opens a browser, signs in, adds an item to a basket and checks the confirmation page. Which level is it?
choices: A unit test, since a basket is a single small feature in the shop
An integration test, since a page asks a server for some data
An end-to-end test, since it walks a whole user flow from start
A unit test, since only one user is taking part in the test
items.explanation: Driving a real browser through a whole flow is the end-to-end level, however small the feature feels.

A missing check for negative numbers inside the function
A mistake in how one calculation rounds its final total
Two parts disagreeing on the data format between them
items.explanation: A unit test isolates the function from its neighbours, so a disagreement on the boundary between components is invisible to it.

items.prompt: A colleague says end-to-end tests are the real tests and the others are warm-ups. Which reply is accurate?
choices: Correct, since only they prove that the product works
Not quite: each level catches problems others cannot see
Correct, since the lower levels never find any real bugs
Not quite: end-to-end tests are pointless once units exist
items.explanation: Each level owns a class of problem. End-to-end tests see the whole flow but are slow and vague, while unit tests are fast and precise but narrow.

items.prompt: In a healthy pyramid, which level has the most tests?
choices: End-to-end
Integration
Unit
They are equal in number
items.explanation: Unit tests are cheap and precise, so there are many of them at the base.

items.prompt: In a healthy pyramid, which level has the fewest tests?
choices: Unit
Integration
They are equal in number
End-to-end
items.explanation: End-to-end tests are the slowest and the least reliable, so only a few are kept.

items.prompt: What is the pyramid's shape based on?
choices: The cost of each kind of test
A fixed industry law
The age of the codebase
The number of developers
items.explanation: Cheaper tests are written in volume and costlier ones sparingly, so the shape follows from cost.

items.prompt: What is an upside-down pyramid, or ice cream cone?
choices: A suite made up only of unit tests
A suite with mostly e2e tests and few unit tests
A suite that has no tests at the top level
A suite in which every test is run twice
items.explanation: It inverts the pyramid: the heavy, slow level holds the bulk of the tests.

items.prompt: In this unit's assumed timings, how long does one end-to-end test take?
choices: 50 ms
3 hours
items.explanation: The unit assumes 50 ms for a unit test, 1.5 s for an integration test and 12 s for an end-to-end test.

items.prompt: What are two main problems with a suite that is mostly end-to-end tests?
choices: It is slow and fails for unrelated reasons
It is too fast and too precise to be useful
It uses too little memory on the machine
It cannot run on more than one computer
items.explanation: Many moving parts per test make the suite slow and prone to failures that are not real bugs.

items.prompt: For 500 tests with 60% end-to-end, the assumed runtime is about what?
choices: About 8 minutes
About 3 minutes
About 61 minutes
About 12 hours
items.explanation: 300 e2e tests at 12 s alone take 60 minutes, plus a little for the other 200.

items.prompt: How is the pyramid best described?
choices: A legal requirement for test suites
A shape that follows from cost, not a rule
A rule every project must follow to the letter
A tool that writes tests automatically
items.explanation: It is a guide that comes from the cost and confidence trade-off.

items.prompt: Two 500-test suites cover the same behaviours: one with 5% end-to-end tests, one with 60%. Which statement is true under the assumed timings?
choices: The 5% suite takes about 7.7 minutes, the 60% one about 61
Both take about the same time, since both hold 500 tests
The 60% suite runs faster, since e2e tests run in parallel
The 5% suite takes longer, since it holds more unit tests
items.explanation: Runtime depends on the mix: 300 e2e tests at 12 s dominate the 60% suite.
items.reference:
500 tests, two shapes (assumed timings)
pyramid, 5% e2e: 380 / 95 / 25, about 7.7 min
upside-down, 60% e2e: 160 / 40 / 300, about 61 min
unit 50 ms, integration 1.5 s, e2e 12 s per test
Why: the pyramid keeps the cheap tests in volume and the costly ones few.
items.learnMore:
Why the shape is a pyramid

Per-test cost rises from unit to integration to end-to-end, both in running time and in unrelated failures. So a sensible suite buys the cheap level in volume and the expensive level sparingly. The shape follows from cost, not from a rule of nature.

Common mistake

Thinking more end-to-end tests means more safety. For the same behaviours it only means more time and more failures that have nothing to do with the code.
items.reflection: Think of any inspection you do at several scales, such as proofreading a document. Where do you spend most of your effort and where do you spend the least, and why?

items.prompt: A team's suite takes 40 minutes and often fails for no real reason. Their plan is to add 200 more end-to-end tests for safety. What is the best critique?
choices: It is fine, since adding more tests always means more safety
It adds time and unrelated failures with no new behaviour
It is fine as long as the new tests are written very carefully
It would only help if the new tests were also made slower
items.explanation: Extra tests at the costly level add runtime and flakiness. Safety comes from covering the right behaviours at the cheapest level that can see them.

items.prompt: If unit and integration tests exist, why keep any end-to-end tests at all?
choices: Because they are the cheapest tests to write and maintain
Because they are the fastest tests to run in the pipeline
Because lower levels cannot see if the flow works for users
Because they remove the need to find the cause of failures
items.explanation: Some failures only show when the whole flow runs, such as a page that never shows the right total. Only the top level can catch those.

items.prompt: In the 5% pyramid, e2e tests are 5% of the tests but about 65% of the runtime. What does this suggest?
choices: The layer is cheap, so it should be expanded greatly
Runtime does not depend on the level of the test at all
The unit layer should be removed to save a lot of time
Each test is costly, so the layer must stay small and chosen
items.explanation: 25 tests at 12 s each is 300 s out of about 461 s. Even a handful of e2e tests carries most of the bill.

items.prompt: Which level gives the most precise failure message?
choices: Integration
End-to-end
Unit
All three are equal
items.explanation: A unit test covers one small thing, so its failure points straight at it.

items.prompt: Why are end-to-end tests the most fragile?
choices: They depend on the most moving parts
They use the simplest code of the three
They contain the fewest checks of the three
They never touch a network at all
items.explanation: More parts per test means more ways to fail for reasons unrelated to the change.

items.prompt: What can an integration test see that a unit test cannot?
choices: A typo inside one function
Whether real parts agree on how they talk
Whether a colour looks right on a screen
How many users are online right now
items.explanation: Integration tests run real components together, so they can reveal a mismatched contract between them.

items.prompt: Which level gives the vaguest failure message?
choices: Unit
Integration
They are equal
End-to-end
items.explanation: An end-to-end failure usually says only that a flow is broken, and the cause still needs a hunt.

items.prompt: Which level is the fastest?
choices: Unit
Integration
End-to-end
They are equal
items.explanation: Unit tests run in milliseconds because they start almost nothing.

items.prompt: Does re-writing a pure-function check as an end-to-end test let it find new bugs?
choices: Yes, since it runs more code
No, it only gets slower and vaguer
Yes, since it runs in a real browser
No, since browsers cannot run tests
items.explanation: The same logic is tested either way. The higher level adds cost, not detection.

items.prompt: Two suites cover the same behaviours at different levels. What mainly differs between them?
choices: The behaviours they cover
The number of features in the product
The cost to run and to trust them
The programming language they use
items.explanation: Coverage is the same, so the difference is runtime, precision and unrelated failures.

items.prompt: Why is "it catches the bug" not enough to choose a level?
choices: Speed, precision and fragility also differ by level
Bugs are very rare in practice
Each level catches a different number of bugs
Only slow tests can ever be trusted
items.explanation: The level fixes several properties at once, not just whether the bug is caught.

items.prompt: The same bug is caught by a 2 ms unit test or a 6 minute e2e test. Besides speed, what else does the unit test offer?
choices: It tests a larger part of the system in a single run
It also guards against problems with the browser itself
It names the broken function rather than a failed flow
It needs no code to be written before it can be run
items.explanation: A narrow test fails narrowly, so the cause is known at once. The e2e failure still needs a search.
items.reference:
Four rows, three levels
speed: ms / seconds / seconds to minutes
failure message: names a function / a boundary / "the flow broke"
unrelated failures: low / moderate / high
coverage for the same behaviours: no difference by level
Why: a level fixes speed, precision and fragility together, so catching the bug is only one of the properties.
items.learnMore:
Why the level matters beyond catching the bug

Speed, precision and fragility change with the level. A higher level does not detect more for the same behaviour. It only adds runtime, vaguer failures and more unrelated failures.

Common mistake

Choosing a level because it feels more thorough, when the bug would have been caught equally well lower down.
items.reflection: Think of a decision you made by a slow, broad check where a quick, narrow one would have done. What did the broad check cost you, and what did it fail to tell you?

items.prompt: A suite fails nightly on a different e2e test each time, and nobody investigates. Which property is at work and what is the likely result?
choices: Fragility, so real regressions hide among the noise
Speed, so the tests finish before anyone gets to look
Precision, so every failure points at exactly the same line
Coverage, so too many behaviours end up tested twice
items.explanation: Frequent unrelated failures teach people to dismiss red runs, and a real regression then hides among them.

choices: Slow startup of the browser window in the pipeline
Too many unit tests running at the same time
A lack of integration tests anywhere in the suite
Triage time spent finding the failed component
items.explanation: Low failure specificity means someone has to work out which part of the flow is responsible before fixing anything.

items.prompt: Rounding a price to two decimals belongs at which level?
choices: Unit
Integration
End-to-end
No test is needed
items.explanation: It is pure logic in isolated code.

items.prompt: Checking that the checkout code and the payment service agree on the response format belongs at which level?
choices: Unit
End-to-end
Integration
No test is needed
items.explanation: A contract between two real components is an integration question.

items.prompt: Checking that a new user can sign up and reach their dashboard belongs at which level?
choices: Unit
Integration
No test is needed
End-to-end
items.explanation: It is a critical flow that crosses the whole system.

items.prompt: A function must reject an empty string. Which level is best?
choices: End-to-end
Unit
Integration
Load level
items.explanation: One function's behaviour, no neighbours involved: unit.

items.prompt: What question does the decision chart start with?
choices: What would make this test fail?
Which tool do I know best?
How long will this take to write?
Which level is the newest?
items.explanation: The cause of failure you want to catch decides the level.

items.prompt: Which is a bad reason to choose an end-to-end test?
choices: It checks a critical user flow
It feels more thorough
Nothing lower down can see this problem
It covers a flow that crosses many parts
items.explanation: Feeling thorough is not a cause of failure. It is a habit and often points at the wrong level.

items.prompt: A real database query must return rows in the shape the code expects. Which level?
choices: Integration
Unit
End-to-end
No test is needed
items.explanation: Two real components, the code and the database, must agree.

items.prompt: How many end-to-end tests should critical flows get?
choices: One for every function
None at all
A small, deliberate handful
As many as possible
items.explanation: They are costly, so they are kept for flows that matter most.

items.prompt: A shipping fee total is off by one cent because of how a fraction is rounded. Which level should own the test for this?
choices: End-to-end, since the fee is shown on the checkout page
Integration, since the fee gets stored in a database
Unit, since the cause lies in one pure calculation
None, since a difference of one cent is not worth a test
items.explanation: The cause is in one pure function, so the cheapest, most precise level is unit. The page merely displays the result.
items.reference:
What would make this test fail?
logic error in isolated code: unit
two real components disagree on a contract: integration
a critical whole user flow breaks: e2e, kept few
Why: let the cause you want to catch pick the level, not habit or comfort.
items.learnMore:
Picking the level

Ask what specifically would make the test fail. A pure logic error belongs at unit level. A mismatch between real components belongs at integration level. A broken critical flow belongs in a small number of end-to-end tests.

Common mistake

Choosing the level you are most comfortable writing, or the one that feels most thorough, rather than the one the cause points to.
items.reflection: Think of a problem you tend to check the same way every time. What question could you ask first to pick a more fitting check?

items.prompt: After a service upgrade, order totals show blank because the service renamed a field the checkout reads. Which level should own a dedicated test?
choices: Integration, since two real parts disagree on a contract
Unit, since the checkout code has a function reading the field
End-to-end, since only a browser can display blank totals
None, since upgrades are always tested by the vendor
items.explanation: The cause is two real components disagreeing. A unit test with a stand-in would keep passing, and an e2e test would hide where the break is.

choices: A unit test
An integration test
An end-to-end test
A security audit
items.explanation: It isolates your code from the other component, which is the definition of a unit test.

items.prompt: Why can a contract mismatch slip past a test that uses a stand-in?

The stand-in is too slow to be useful
The stand-in runs on a different computer
Stand-ins cannot be written down in code
items.explanation: The stand-in never changes, even when the real component does.

items.prompt: Where does a stand-in's answer shape come from?
choices: The real service
The network cable
Whoever wrote the stand-in
The database engine
items.explanation: It reflects an assumption, which is exactly what can go out of date.

items.prompt: Are stand-ins acceptable inside unit tests?
choices: No, they must never be used
Only in end-to-end tests
Only on weekends

items.explanation: Unit tests want isolation, so replacing neighbours is normal.

items.prompt: What does a genuine integration test contact?
choices: A stand-in written by the author
A real, maybe local and throwaway, instance
Only the test runner itself
Nothing outside the test file
items.explanation: It needs the real thing, or no real boundary is being crossed.

items.prompt: A suite of green integration tests missed a contract mismatch. What should you check first?
choices: How many tests there are
What font the report uses
What the tests actually call
Which day they were run
items.explanation: If the calls go to stand-ins, the suite was never testing the boundary.

items.prompt: Which bug can a stand-in never reveal?
choices: A typo in your own function
A missing check for empty input
A wrong total in your calculation
The real part changing its answer
items.explanation: Only the real component can show that its answer changed.

items.prompt: Why do we keep an integration layer between unit and e2e tests?
choices: Units cannot cross real boundaries and e2e hides the cause
Unit tests are always wrong
E2E tests are never allowed to fail
It makes the whole suite shorter
items.explanation: The middle layer catches contract problems precisely, without the cost of the whole flow.

items.prompt: All 200 tests stub the discount service. The service renames a field and every test stays green, yet checkout shows no discounts. What explains this?
choices: The tests never called the real service, so its change stayed hidden
The tests were too slow to notice that anything had changed there
The tests ran at unit level, which is always less accurate than others
The tests relied on too many real databases being present at once
items.explanation: A stand-in keeps answering in the old shape. Only a real call would have received the new one.
items.reference:
Does the real thing answer?
stand-in answers: a unit test wearing another name
real throwaway instance answers: a genuine integration test
stand-in shape = an author's assumption
Why: a test can only protect a boundary it actually crosses.
items.learnMore:
Fake integration tests

If the other component is replaced by a stand-in, the test checks your code against a guess about that component. Stand-ins are fine inside unit tests. They only become a problem when the suite is called integration coverage and relied on for boundary safety.

Common mistake

Counting green tests instead of asking what answers the call. A large suite of stubbed tests can stay green while the real contract drifts.
items.reflection: Think of a rehearsal you ran with a stand-in for someone important. What did the real person do that the stand-in never could?

items.prompt: Which review question best exposes a fake integration test?
choices: How many assertions does the test contain in total?
How long does the test file take to open in an editor?
Does it use one of the most popular test runners?
Could the real part change its answer without a failure here?
items.explanation: If the answer is yes, the boundary is unprotected, whatever the test is called.

items.prompt: A partner's service cannot be started locally. Which approach keeps the most boundary protection?
choices: Delete the boundary tests and rely on end-to-end tests alone
Check the partner's sandbox and keep stand-ins matching it
Stub the service forever and never look at its real answers
Test only the happy path against the stand-in answers
items.explanation: Some real contact with the partner, even occasional, keeps the stand-ins honest. Pure stand-ins drift.

It starts a local discount service and runs checkout on it
It asserts only that the checkout function exists in the code
It replays a saved answer recorded a year ago on a laptop
items.explanation: Only a live service can answer in whatever shape it currently uses.

items.prompt: Implement `suiteRuntimeMs(units, integrations, e2es)`: total running time in milliseconds, using 50 ms per unit test, 1500 ms per integration test and 12000 ms per e2e test.
items.explanation: Each level contributes its count times its per-test time, and the three contributions add up.

items.prompt: Implement `e2ePercent(total, e2e)`: the percentage of tests that are end-to-end, as a number between 0 and 100.
items.explanation: Multiplying by 100 before dividing keeps these whole-number cases exact, with no rounding noise.

items.prompt: Implement `splitRest(rest)`: divide the non-e2e tests 80/20 between unit and integration tests. Round the integration count to a whole number and give unit tests the remainder. Return `{ unit, integration }`.
items.explanation: Computing the integration share first and subtracting guarantees the two counts always add up to the total.

items.prompt: Implement `perTestMs(level)`: 50 for "unit", 1500 for "integration", 12000 for "e2e". Throw an error for any other value.
items.explanation: A lookup table holds the assumed costs, and an explicit error stops an unknown level from silently becoming undefined.

items.prompt: Implement `countByLevel(tests)`. Each test is `{ level }` with level "unit", "integration" or "e2e". Return `{ unit, integration, e2e }` with the counts.

tests.expr: expect(countByLevel([{ level: "unit" }, { level: "e2e" }, { level: "unit" }])).toEqual({ unit: 2, integration: 0, e2e: 1 })

items.explanation: Start every count at zero so levels with no tests still appear, then add one per test.

items.prompt: Implement `isUpsideDown(unit, integration, e2e)`: return true when there are more end-to-end tests than unit tests.
items.explanation: The shape is inverted when the costly top level outnumbers the cheap base. Equal counts are not inverted.

items.prompt: Implement `toMinutes(ms)`: convert milliseconds to minutes.
items.explanation: A minute is 60 seconds of 1000 ms each, so divide by 60000.

items.prompt: Implement `slowestLevel(units, integrations, e2es)`: return which level ("unit", "integration" or "e2e") contributes the most total time, using 50 ms, 1500 ms and 12000 ms per test.
items.explanation: Total time per level is count times cost, so even a small count of e2e tests can dominate. Keep the level with the largest total.

items.prompt: Implement `chanceOfFlake(p, n)`: the chance that at least one of `n` independent tests fails for no real reason, when each one does so with chance `p` (a number between 0 and 1).
items.explanation: A run is clean only when every test is clean, which has chance (1 - p)^n. The chance of at least one flake is the complement. Multiplying p by n would overcount and could pass 100%.
items.reference:
Flaky chances compound
one test flakes with chance p
n tests: chance of at least one = 1 - (1 - p)^n
p = 0.6%: n = 25 gives about 14%, n = 300 about 84%
Why: a run is clean only if every single test is clean, so small odds multiply.
items.learnMore:
Counting runtime and flakes

Runtime is a plain weighted sum of the number of tests at each level. Flakiness compounds: the chance that every test is clean is the product of the individual chances, so the chance of at least one failure is one minus that product.

Common mistake

Multiplying p by n. That overcounts, and it can even exceed 100%.
items.reflection: Think of a chain of steps, each one very likely to work. How likely is the whole chain to work, and what would you do to shorten it?

items.prompt: Implement `projectedRuntimeMs(total, e2ePercent)`: for a suite of `total` tests where `e2ePercent` percent are e2e (rounded to a whole number of tests), split the rest 80/20 between unit and integration tests (integration rounded to a whole number, unit gets the remainder). Use 50, 1500 and 12000 ms per test and return the total in ms.
items.explanation: Work out the e2e count first, split the remainder 80/20, then weight each count by its per-test time. Computing the integration count first and subtracting keeps the three counts summing to the total.

items.prompt: Implement `maxE2ETests(p, limit)`: the largest number of e2e tests `n` such that the chance of at least one unrelated failure, 1 - (1 - p)^n, stays at or below `limit`.
items.explanation: Keep adding one test while the chance of at least one flake still fits the limit, and stop at the first test that would break it. This turns the compounding formula into a budget for how large the e2e layer can be.
